column3: Brief enjoyment before guilt and consequence echoes the focus's limited interval, without the return after relief.
Affliction is removed until an appointed term and the people immediately break their pledge, directly paralleling relief followed by relapse.
When harm is removed, some return to associating partners, closely matching the focus's exposure of entrenched conduct after relief.
It announces painful punishment but supplies neither its temporary removal nor a renewed response.
The plea to remove the punishment is the immediate request answered by the focus, framing its brief reprieve.
It treats returning to an earlier utterance as a repeated practice requiring repair, illuminating the focus's habitual return without its relief sequence.
A short enjoyment followed by severe punishment parallels the focus's limited interval and coming consequence.
It opens the immediate passage by announcing the visible smoke that becomes the punishment briefly lifted in the focus.
Its small portion of the night is unrelated to punishment, relief, or returning to wrongdoing.
Its short duration concerns earthly residence, not a reprieve that reveals recurrence.
Moses' invocation against a criminal people belongs to the next movement of the same passage, contrasting the preceding plea for relief.
Divine beginning and restoring provide a broad sense of return but not the focus's behavioral relapse.

It identifies the smoke as painful punishment in the immediate sequence leading to the focus's temporary lifting.
The rain and resurrection image does not address relief from punishment or a return to prior conduct.
It affirms that only God can remove the approaching calamity, supporting the focus's divine removal of punishment.
Removal of a covering reveals what was hidden, conceptually resonating with relief as disclosure but without relapse.
The small number who believe follows covenant-breaking, but it lacks the focus's relief-and-return structure.
Shared punishment of wrongdoers gives only a general consequence for the conduct exposed in the focus.
The great seizure and vengeance complete the immediate warning after the brief removal and return announced in the focus.
Even if returned, they would return to what they were forbidden, directly articulating the persistence of conduct in the focus.

A slight inclination and divine stabilization offer a distant contrast to recurring deviation after pressure lifts.

Under affliction the people promise belief if it is removed, providing the direct prelude to 7:135's broken pledge.
The small number of later people has no thematic role in the focus.
Death is a broad later consequence, not a temporary lifting of punishment or behavioral return.
Minimal remembrance and performative prayer show inwardly thin commitment, a loose analogue to relapse after pressure ends.
The condemned ask to be released and conditionally acknowledge future return to wrongdoing, closely echoing recurrence though not actual relief.
The declaration of loss does not clarify the focus's cycle.
Giving little and stopping concerns interrupted generosity, not the temporary removal and return at issue.
The report that Ad denied messengers has no specific relation beyond generic disbelief.
God answers the distressed and removes harm, clarifying the divine relief in the focus while omitting the relapse.
Punishment of hostile figures does not involve a prior reprieve or return.
The mention of Ad is not a meaningful use of return or relief here.
Conflicting speech does not illuminate the focus's punishment-and-relapse pattern.
Reduced perception and the return of all matters to God offer only a distant connection through briefness and return.
The warning against following protectors and scant remembrance generally addresses failure to remain guided.
Return to earth and emergence describe a physical cycle, not a return to sinful conduct after reprieve.
Scarce gratitude despite bestowed faculties loosely supports the focus's diagnosis of persistent unresponsiveness.
Return after creation is an eschatological return, distinct from the focus's recurrence of behavior.
Ad's denial and punishment supply a general warning context but no relief or relapse sequence.
Its threatened expulsion of hypocrites does not bear on the focus's cycle.
It explicitly makes renewed wrongdoing meet renewed punishment, strongly clarifying the focus's announced return.
Trading divine signs for a small price is a specific form of wrongdoing, but no relief-and-return sequence appears.
Punishment fails to produce humility or supplication, closely depicting the resistant disposition that the focus exposes after relief.
It forbids ever returning to the same offense, treating return as a recurrent ethical pattern rather than a one-time act.
Re-creation after the first creation uses a different, cosmic sense of return.
Even if mercy removed their harm, they would persist blindly in rebellion, directly matching relief that leaves entrenched conduct intact.
A person calls on God in harm, then forgets and associates partners after receiving favor, a close individual parallel to the focus.
Earlier communities reject their messengers, offering only a broad pattern of persistent disbelief.
The plea for the punishment's removal and promise of guidance is the immediate prelude to the broken pledge in 43:50.
The bare mention of Ad, Pharaoh, and Lot's people does not illuminate the focus.
Divine vengeance against them continues the Pharaoh narrative but is less direct than the relief-and-relapse pair.
The appointed gathering of messengers has no relevant connection.
The destruction of the former Ad does not contribute a relief or relapse parallel.
The command for Moses to depart follows the focus passage, providing narrative continuation but not its central cycle.
Failure to believe in God is only a generic cause of punishment.
Closed hearts and scarce belief suggest entrenched rejection, but without the focus's temporary respite.
Flight to God is a corrective alternative to the return to wrongdoing foretold in the focus.
Entry into Hell has no specific relation to relief or recurrence.
After receiving admonition, whoever returns to usury faces the Fire; it gives a clear legal-ethical instance of relapse.
The address to deniers does not add a distinctive connection.
God's guidance and vengeance give a general divine-authority frame for the focus's warning.
The resurrection call and perceived short stay concern a different return and a different sense of little.

The challenge to act in one's position does not clarify the focus's cycle.
Recreating creation is a cosmic repetition, distinct from behavioral relapse after punishment is lifted.
The refusal of aid after the fact supplies a general punitive consequence, not temporary relief.
The oath by this city has no relevant connection.
Selling signs for a small price describes wrongdoing but not the focus's removal and renewed return.
The warning about obeying a human messenger is unrelated to the focus.
A stated willingness collapses when the commanded trial arrives, paralleling commitment that proves conditional under pressure.
Resurrection provides a broad future consequence for human conduct, not the focus's immediate pattern.
Describing a group as few has no thematic relation to the focus's little reprieve.
They return to themselves and acknowledge wrongdoing, a contrasting moment of recognition rather than return to prior sin.
Creation, re-creation, and return to God use a cosmic and eschatological sense of return.
The denial of future punishment contrasts with the focus's certainty that punishment will return.
A small group remains faithful through a test, contrasting with the focus's failure to sustain change after pressure.
The accusation in Joseph's story does not illuminate the focus.
The small amount of human knowledge is unrelated to a brief removal of punishment.

God's power to begin and repeat creation concerns a distinct sense of repetition.
The warning that Moses' followers will be pursued does not address the focus's cycle.
A possible return to sea punishment after disbelief is a loose recurrence of consequence, not relief followed by relapse.

Divine protection from mockers is unrelated to removing punishment and return.
The comparison of helpers and numbers does not illuminate the focus.
It commands turning back to God before punishment comes, the needed alternative to the focus's foretold return to wrongdoing.
The moon's recurrent phase is unrelated to moral relapse or temporary relief.
Scarce gratitude after divine gifts loosely reflects a persistent failure to change, without the focus's sequence.
Worldly enjoyment is little beside the Hereafter, a limited temporal contrast rather than relief and relapse.
The weighty word has no meaningful relation to the focus.
A short delay before judgment resembles a limited reprieve, but it does not show return to prior conduct.
The prayer to avert Hell's punishment relates generally to removal of punishment but lacks the focus's return.
It denies that alleged partners can remove or redirect harm, clarifying the exclusive agency behind the focus's removal.
Distress at sea makes people call on God, but after He delivers them to land they turn away, directly matching relief followed by reversal.
When harm is removed, the person passes on as though he had never called for relief, a close individual parallel to the focus.
Those in a sea storm promise grateful devotion if saved, supplying the conditional plea that precedes the relapse in the next verse.
After God saves them, they transgress on earth, directly portraying wrongdoing resumed after rescue.
They call sincerely on God in danger at sea, then associate partners once He delivers them to land.
The plea for deliverance from layered distress promises gratitude, closely paralleling the focus's request for relief under pressure.
God delivers them from every distress, yet they return to associating partners, explicitly joining relief to relapse.
After mercy follows adversity, a person claims the evils have gone and becomes exultant, showing how relief can expose a false settled response.
After mercy follows adversity, people scheme against God's signs, directly showing misconduct after relief.
When harm drives people to call on their Lord and He lets them taste mercy, some immediately associate partners again.
A person calls on God in harm, then attributes the granted favor to personal knowledge, a close reversal after relief.
After mercy follows adversity, the recipient claims entitlement and denies accountability, displaying relapse after favor.
When favor is bestowed, the human turns away, while harm brings urgent supplication; this describes the same conditional disposition.
God tests a people with good and bad conditions so that they might return, presenting the corrective purpose absent from the focus's relapse.
Hardship and adversity are sent so a town may humble itself, providing the pressure-response frame of the focus.
Adversity is replaced with good conditions, after which heedlessness remains and sudden seizure follows, a related warning about relief without reform.
Pharaoh's people are seized with years of drought and shortage so that they might remember, establishing the punitive setting of their later broken pledges.
The escalating signs of punishment against Pharaoh's people form the affliction sequence that produces their temporary promises of change.
Their eventual drowning after denying signs completes the consequence for the same community that repeatedly broke commitments after relief.
The signs and punishments are successively intensified so that Pharaoh's people might return, directly framing the pleas of 43:49-50.
Earlier communities are seized with misery and hardship so they may humble themselves, supplying a broad pressure-and-response parallel.
Even under misery and hardship they do not humble themselves, depicting the hardened disposition diagnosed by the focus.
After forgetting admonition, abundant openings are granted before sudden seizure, a related warning that ease need not produce reform.
The nearer punishment is made to be tasted so that people may return, giving the intended corrective alternative to the focus's announced return to sin.
People are made to taste some consequence of what they earned so that they may return, closely linking affliction with a hoped-for change of conduct.
They are tested once or twice each year, yet neither repent nor take heed, a direct pattern of repeated warning without inward change.
When the affluent are seized with punishment they cry out, supplying the distress-driven plea that the focus shows to be temporary.
A severe punishment leaves them despairing, continuing the same passage's contrast between cries under pressure and durable transformation.
All favor is from God, and harm makes people cry to Him; it supplies the antecedent pattern to 16:54's relapse after removal.
No one but God can remove harm, directly supporting the divine agency that temporarily removes punishment in the focus.
When people finally see divine punishment, they profess belief, a contrast showing that a response elicited by punishment may come too late.
Belief after seeing punishment does not benefit them, underscoring the consequence of delayed or merely pressure-driven response.
Faith at the arrival of decisive signs does not benefit one who had not believed before, a related limit on responses forced by impending punishment.
One who worships only while receiving good turns away when tried, expressing the same conditional and unstable allegiance exposed by the focus.
Human beings turn away when grace reaches them and call urgently when evil touches them, a concise description of the focus's conditional disposition.
